en: Preface to the Essentials of Cultivating the West:
The moment one knows the past, it has already been replaced by the present; the moment one knows the present, it has already been replaced by the future.
Such transformations occur such that not a single kṣaṇa remains stationary. Yet, while every moment undergoes change, the ocean of Amitābha’s vows remains unchanging.
Furthermore, while every thought-moment undergoes transformation, the name of Amitābha does not transform. Having thoroughly penetrated the past and the future, he is called Amitābha Buddha.
He is currently preaching the Dharma. At the time he preaches the Dharma, it is the very moment of his present reception;
at the moment of his present reception, it is the very moment of his present bestowal of prophecy. There is not a single place where he does not manifest, nor is there another...
The place [of rebirth] is not fixed. For this reason, Master Lianchi’s final instruction was: "Recite the Buddha's name with sincerity; do not change the subject.
Not only must one not change the practice of reciting the Buddha's name, but even "sincerity" itself must not be changed.

At the critical juncture of birth and death for a human being, one is about to exchange this segmented physical body for a *antarābhava* (intermediate state) body—how perilous! If one does not maintain the same subject during ordinary times, at the moment of life...
One will certainly not undergo the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Why is this? Because when one reaches the ultimate of sincerity, one immediately attains the power of the Buddha.
When the Buddha’s power manifests before one, one’s mindfulness of the Buddha becomes complete. One abandons the Sahā world and is born in Sukhāvatī without any transition;

by relying on the Buddha’s power, one is transformed into a lotus womb. Master Xina had been in accord with [the Dharma] for many years; throughout his life, he recited the Buddha’s name with a pure heart, maintaining it with constant intimacy.
Without ceasing, he utilized his leisure time from his pure devotions to compile the Pure Land teachings of the ancient masters, gathering them together into this volume.
Upon examining what he has compiled, it perfectly accords with the theory in Zhiyi’s *Ten Doubts* regarding faith in the power of others (*parāśraya*).

For those who rely on their own power (*svabala*), it seems easy but is actually difficult; for those who rely on the power of others, it seems difficult but is actually easy. May beginners, perhaps by means of this compilation, [attain realization].
Having gained right knowledge and right view through the initial words of entry, one deeply believes in the Dharma-gate of Other-Power.
By relinquishing body and mind and upholding the Name, there is never a lack of some small benefit for the practitioner; for this reason, I have compiled this as my own record.
It may serve as a warning and exhortation. Since this is precisely for mutual exhortation, why should it not be acceptable?

Written on the first day of the tenth month in the tenth year of the Guangxu era by the student of Pure Land practice, Benpu, who reverently composed this "Essentials for Cultivating the Western Paradise."
Compiled by the Monk Xinan of Wulin.
The True Cause of the Ten Recitations.
The Eighteenth Vow of Amitābha Buddha states: "If there are sentient beings who desire to be born in my land, they shall with a sincere heart believe..."
Joy. Even down to ten recitations—if [the Pure Land] were not brought forth, I would not attain perfect enlightenment. The practitioner simply needs to have sufficient faith;

they must believe that through these ten recitations, they will certainly enter the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s vows, such that naturally, thought after thought, they are in resonance with the Buddha.
Such power of faith and such power of mindfulness rely entirely upon the power of Amitābha’s vows. Relying on Amitābha...
Dhāraṇī. Because it is certain to produce [rebirth], these ten recitations are inconceivable. As for the gateway of the ten recitations:
every morning, after dressing and finishing one's attire, stand upright facing west, join the palms, and invoke the name of Amitābha Buddha. Complete a single breath as one recitation.

Thus, ten breaths constitute ten recitations (*daśa-smṛti*). One follows the length of the breaths without being restricted by a fixed number of Buddhas; the limit is reached when the breath is exhausted.
The voice should be neither too high nor too low, neither too slow nor too hurried, but balanced and moderate. Ten breaths are to be continuous, keeping the mind from scattering;

making this focused application of effort is called the "Method of Ten Recitations. Having performed these recitations, one should then single-mindedly recite the text for taking refuge in the World of Ultimate Bliss.

(Appended is the prayer text. Regarding this method for fixed recitation: whether at two periods (morning and evening), three periods, or six periods, the practitioner should cultivate it according to their capacity.
If one is traveling on a journey and lacks the convenience of washing hands and burning incense, one should first recite "Oṃ-lam" (this mantra of the Pure Dharma-realm) seven times.
Facing the western direction, silently maintain ten recitations and single-mindedly take refuge with the prayer text.

In one's daily practice of pure deeds, one should regularly recite the *Smaller Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra*. This text clearly demonstrates that through faith, aspiration, and the holding of the Name, one may directly ascend to the stage of non-retrogression.
Yet, while this Name is very easy to hold, it is extremely difficult to believe. Without decisive faith, there can be no decisive aspiration. As the Sūtra says: "You all..."
All sentient beings should believe this. Furthermore, it is said: "For the sake of all sentient beings, I have preached this Dharma that is difficult for the world to believe.
Our Buddha’s compassion is thorough and profound; he thus exhorts people to believe and accept it.

When sentient beings hear this sutra, once they have believed it, they shall never again harbor doubts; this is precisely the causal condition of many roots of goodness and merit. They possess resolute faith.
I pray that people will rise early every morning to practice the method of ten recitations. Furthermore, they must maintain the holding of the Buddha’s name and increase their regular devotions.
As for the regular devotions: at the two times of morning and evening, one should burn incense and prostrate before the Buddha, reciting one scroll of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Recite the *Ōjōju* (Rebirth Mantra) three times and the *Nenbutsu Ge* (Buddha-Recitation Verse) once.

Then, taking up the prayer beads, recite the name of Amida Buddha—either one thousand, three thousand, or five thousand times. Upon completion, perform the dedication of merit and make vows before the Buddha by reciting the text "With Single-Minded Devotion, I Take Refuge in the World of Ultimate Bliss.
In this manner, one must constantly practice with diligence every day without interruption.
[Severance] (The Sūtra and Dhāraṇī are recorded in the *Gongke Ben*; the Ritual for Reciting the Buddha’s Name is appended below).
Regarding the method of reciting the Buddha’s name as a practice of counting and maintaining [the count] (an excerpt from the *Wuliangyi Dashi Yulu*):

There is nothing particularly extraordinary about the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation; it simply values being able to believe thoroughly and maintain it steadily, proceeding directly with the recitation.
Whether it be one hundred thousand, fifty thousand, or thirty thousand recitations per day and night, take as the standard a fixed number performed without fail.
Vow that for the remainder of this life you shall never change your resolve. If you do not attain rebirth there, then the Buddhas of the three periods of time would be speaking falsehoods.
Once rebirth is attained, you shall never again fall back. All manner of Dharma gates will manifest before you. You must by all means avoid [distraction] today.

Third: Tomorrow, when meeting Li Si, one thinks of the teachings of the schools; when meeting those of the Chan school, one thinks of searching for poetic lines; when meeting those who investigate through question-and-answer, one thinks of the principles of inquiry;
and when meeting those who uphold the Vinaya, one thinks of donning robes and using the alms bowl. In this way, every encounter remains unresolved and every account remains unsettled.
How could one know that by reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha until it is matured, the three piṭakas and twelve divisions of the canon, as well as the thousand [scriptures], are all mastered?
The seven hundred koans, the three thousand codes of dignified conduct, and the eighty thousand subtle practices are all contained herein.

To truly practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name is to set aside the world of body and mind; this is itself the Great Dāna. To truly practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name is to no longer give rise to greed, anger, or delusion.
This is great upholding of the precepts; truly being able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, without calculating right and wrong or self and others. This is great patience;

truly being able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, without even the slightest interruption or admixture of other thoughts. This is great vigor; truly being able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, no longer allowing deluded thoughts to run wild.
This is great meditative concentration; truly being able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, not being confused by divergent paths. This is great wisdom.
Examine yourself: if the body, mind, and world have not yet been relinquished; if thoughts of greed, anger, and delusion still arise;
if notions of right and wrong, or self and others, still weigh upon your heart; if interruptions, fragmentation, and intermingling have not yet been entirely eliminated;
if discursive thoughts still pursue their objects without ceasing; and if various divergent paths can still delude your will—then this is not true mindfulness of the Buddha.

To reach the state of single-mindedness without distraction, there is no other method: at the very beginning of your practice, you must use a prayer bead rosary to keep your count clear and establish a fixed schedule that is never missed.
After practicing for a long time until it becomes pure and mature, the recitation will become spontaneous, even when you are not consciously thinking of it.

After that, it is acceptable whether you keep count or do not keep count. If, from the very first thought, you insist on speaking only "fine stories," or insist on being "without attachment to forms," regarding the counting of breaths as a trivial matter and fixed recitation as a form of clinging, this is entirely because your faith is not deep and your practice is not vigorous.
Even if you can expound the twelve divisions of the teachings and deliver the seventeen hundred turning words, it is all [in vain].
These are matters pertaining to the shore of birth and death; at the moment of the end of life, they will certainly be of no use.
One must practice based on one's vows (as cited from the *Chewu Chanshi Yulu*).
Within the Pure Land tradition, the vow is paramount. For anyone who possesses a vow, it will ultimately be fulfilled. This is recorded in the *Shenseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Divine Monks).

A certain monk, before a stone Buddha, playfully made a vow, saying: "If I cannot resolve the cycle of birth and death in this life, I vow to become a powerful and majestic great minister in my next life.
Later, he indeed became a great general; such was the fulfillment of a vow made in jest. Even so, it was ultimately realized.
How much more so for a vow issued from the utmost sincerity! Furthermore, there was a monk who was widely versed in the sutras and treatises;
wherever he went, he encountered no one. A companion monk instructed him in the method of creating karmic connections (*kalyāṇamitra*):

they sold his robes and bedding to purchase food, entered a deep forest, placed the food on the ground, and secretly performed incantations and prayers so that insects and birds might eat it. The monk followed these instructions. Twenty days later...
In the final year, he finally opened the Dharma. Those who received his transformation were many and few alike; they were all birds and insects that had come to receive his food.

This power of his vow is inconceivable. If he was still able to use the vows of another to gather those insects and birds, liberating them from their animal state and causing them to enter the human realm, how could he not be able to save himself through his own vows? It was by means of the forty-eight vows that the Buddha [accomplished this].
I have personally attained Buddhahood. The vows I have made perfectly accord with the Buddha’s vow to gather in and deliver sentient beings.
The moment I made my vow was the very moment the Buddha took me into his care; the moment the Buddha took me into his care was the moment of my right mindfulness. Therefore, by the power of my vow—
This is entirely based on the power of the Buddha’s vows and serves as the certain guarantee for rebirth. The practitioner must never omit their morning and evening devotions.
At the final session, after completing the recitation of the Buddha’s name, one should kneel long before the Buddha with palms joined and chant the Forty-Eight Vows.
Then, recite the names of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the Assembly of the Pure Ocean, making vows and dedicating the merit. Alternatively, perform four prostrations.
The Eighteenth Vow brings even greater benefit. This King of Great Vows must be recollected and cherished with earnest and single-minded devotion.
By regularly performing prostrations and recitations, each vow will become clearly manifest.

At the time of the end of life, the King of Vows will spontaneously appear before you, never abandoning you, and lead you forward to protect your rebirth in the Pure Land. (The ritual for prostrating to the Forty-Eight Vows is appended below.)
Dedicated Cultivation for Benefit (Excerpt from the *Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chue Wu*):
"To see the Way and then cultivate the Way; to cultivate the Way and then realize the Way—this is a path shared by all throughout the ages, an immutable and settled doctrine.
Yet, how easy is it to speak of seeing the Way? If one follows the teachings of the Vehicle, one must first undergo a great opening..."
Complete understanding. If one follows the School of the Gate (Zen), one must first penetrate the heavy barrier directly before one can discuss the cultivation of the path;
otherwise, it becomes blind practice and reckless training, inevitably resulting in bumping into walls, striking against barriers, and falling into pits and ditches.
Only the single gate of Pure Land is not like this: from here, passing through ten trillion Buddha-lands to the west, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who currently dwells there preaching the Dharma. Merely by making a vow and holding his name, one will immediately attain rebirth there.
This is a realm personally known and personally seen by the Buddha’s own heart and eyes; it is not something that can be known or seen by the worthy ones and sages of the three vehicles.
One should simply have deep faith and, relying upon this, make a vow and hold the name. This is...
Taking the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as one's own knowledge and vision, there is no need to seek a separate gate of enlightenment.

In other approaches to the cultivation of the Way, one must first attain enlightenment and then cultivate according to the Dharma: gathering the mind to achieve concentration (*samādhi*), giving rise to wisdom (*prajñā*) through concentration, and severing delusions (*kleśa*) through wisdom.
The wisdom thus produced varies in its degree of excellence, and the delusions severed vary in their depth; only after this can one discuss whether there is regression or not.
[They] fall back. Only within this gate of the Pure Land do we rely solely on the mind of faith and aspiration to single-mindedly uphold the Name.

When the upholding reaches the state of "one-pointedness without distraction," the pure karma is fully accomplished. After death, one will certainly attain rebirth there. Once rebirth is attained, one shall never again fall back.
Furthermore, in the cultivation of other paths, one must first repent for one's present karma; if present karma is not repented of—
This would immediately obstruct the Way, leaving no path for further progress. Those who practice the karma of purity attain rebirth while still carrying their karmic burdens;

they do not need to repent for their karma. This is because reciting the Buddha's name even once with a sincere mind can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

Furthermore, in other gateways of cultivation, one must sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). If the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi- and vitarka-kleśa*) are not yet exhausted, then the cycle of segmented existence (*bhavāgra-pratibaddha*) remains.
If birth and death are not exhausted, one cannot escape from this shared land. Only by cultivating pure karma can one transcend horizontally beyond the triple world.
Without severing afflictions, yet departing from this shared realm to be born in that shared realm—once born in that land, the very roots of birth and death are forever severed.
Having been born in that land, one constantly beholds the Buddha and hears the Dharma at all times. As for the robes...
Food, clothing, and dwelling arise spontaneously; water birds and forest trees all preach the Dharma. While residing within this land, one perceives the three higher Pure Lands;
various superior virtuous beings assemble in one place, collectively realizing the three kinds of non-retrogression, and in a single lifetime, they immediately succeed to the rank of Buddha.
Thus, the Gate of the Pure Land is the initial shortcut for seeking the gate of awakening, yet in the end it is not...

One awaits the arising of wisdom; there is no need to repent for past karma, nor is it necessary to sever afflictions. This is the ultimate in brevity and essentiality, the ultimate in directness and swiftness.
When one attains realization and entry, it is the ultimate in vastness and the ultimate in finality. Students should contemplate this with a refined mind and examine it in detail;
do not, out of temporary arrogance, lose sight of this most excellent and greatest benefit.
For those who practice the Pure Land method, if their faith and aspiration are profound (as noted in the *Recorded Sayings* of Master Ouyi and Master Chue-wo),
and if their faith and aspiration are firm and steadfast, they will certainly attain rebirth even with ten recitations or a single recitation at the time of death.
Conversely, if one lacks faith and aspiration, then even if one holds the Name until it is as impervious to wind and rain as a silver wall, [rebirth cannot be attained].
It is like an iron wall; there is no possibility of it being breached. We practitioners of the Pure Land practice must therefore have deep faith and earnest vows.
Because our faith is deep and our vows are earnest, no heterodox teachings can shake or delude us, and no external circumstances or conditions can lead us astray.
If, while we are correctly practicing the Pure Land path, Master Dharma were suddenly to appear before us...
The Master then said, "I possess the Chan that directly points to the human mind and enables one to see one's nature and become a Buddha.
You need only set aside the practice of reciting the Buddha's name, and I shall transmit this Chan to you. However, you must first pay homage to the Patriarch, declaring:
'I have already received the Dharma-door of reciting the Buddha's name from Śākyamuni Tathāgata; I vow to uphold it and never alter it for the rest of my life. Although the Patriarch..."
Regarding this profound and wondrous dhyāna, I dare not violate my original vow.
Even if Śākyamuni Tathāgata were to manifest before me and say, "The Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha that I previously taught was merely a temporary expedient;
now there is a more excellent Dharma-gate that surpasses it. You should set aside mindfulness of the Buddha for a time, and I shall explain this superior Dharma to you," even then I could only—
He bowed his head to the Buddha and addressed him, saying: "I have previously received from the World-Honored One the Dharma-gate of pure practice.
I have made a vow that as long as I draw one more breath, I shall never alter it. Although the Tathāgata possesses supreme teachings, I dare not violate my original oath.
Even if Buddhas and patriarchs were to manifest before me, I would still not change what I believe; how much less so for the delusions and falsehoods of Māras and non-Buddhists?"
How could such teachings possibly shake or confuse one? To be able to believe in this way is what may be called deep faith.
Even if a glowing iron wheel were to spin upon one’s head, one would not, because of that suffering, lose the vow for rebirth [in the Pure Land].

Even if the supreme and exquisite five desires of a Wheel-Turning King were to appear before one, one would not, because of that pleasure, lose the vow for rebirth. Such is the response to both adversity and favor.
If one does not alter one’s vow even when facing the ultimate [extremes], how much less could the minor worldly conditions of favorability and adversity turn the mind?
To be able to make such a vow—this vow may indeed be called earnest.

*Cutting Off Craving and Practicing Truth* (Recorded from the *Collected Sayings of Master Hanshan*) To recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land is fundamentally intended for resolving the great matter of birth and death. Nowadays, people only begin to recite the Buddha’s name when they resolve to resolve this matter of birth and death;
they merely say that the Buddha can resolve birth and death, yet they do not themselves understand what birth and death are.
As for the root and trunk: ultimately, toward what does one direct one's mindfulness? If the mind that recollects the Buddha is severed, the root and trunk of birth and death cannot be attained;
how then can one fully understand birth and death? What is the root and trunk of birth and death? An ancient said:

"If karma is not heavy, one is not born in Saha; if craving is not severed, one is not born in the Pure Land. From this we know that the root of craving is the very root and trunk of birth and death. This is the deduction.
This root of craving does not exist merely in this present life, nor did it exist only in one, two, three, or four lifetimes.
Rather, from time immemorial, throughout birth after birth and body after body, when has there ever been even a single moment when one was temporarily free from this root of craving?
Because the seeds of such craving have accumulated over vast eons and are profoundly deep-seated, birth and death are therefore endless.
Only today have you finally resolved to practice the recitation of the Buddha's name, yet you merely hope to seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land while remaining empty-handed.

You do not even realize that attachment is the very root of birth and death; how could you have ever had a single thought to sever this clinging? Since you do not know the root of birth and death, [you cannot attain liberation].

If you recite the Buddha’s name while simultaneously nurturing the roots of birth and death, then as you practice such recitation, it will have no connection whatsoever with the cycle of birth and death.
When the time comes for your life to end, you will see only the roots of attachment to birth and death manifesting before you;

only then will you realize that the Buddha’s power has been of no avail at all, and by then, it will be too late for regret. Therefore, I exhort those who currently recite the Buddha’s name to first understand this.
Attachment is the root of birth and death. Now, as you recite the Buddha’s name, you must sever this root of attachment in every thought-moment.
In daily life, it manifests before you: when reciting the Buddha’s name while at home, you see children, grandchildren, family affairs, and property;
there is not a single thing that is not an object of attachment. It is as if your entire body were in a pit of fire. Attachment is the sovereign master. [Yet] you recite the Buddha’s name.
This is merely the surface. For instance, when the feelings of a child for its parents manifest before you, turn the light inward and look:
can this single utterance of "Buddha" truly withstand that love? Can it truly sever that love? If you cannot sever that love, [it is not enough].
Ultimately, how can one bring an end to birth and death? Therefore, I exhort those who practice Buddha-recitation: first, you must have a sense of urgency regarding birth and death;
you must have a sense of urgency to sever birth and death. You must, at every moment, cut through the very roots of birth and death.
Then, every thought-moment is a time for ending birth and death. If you maintain such earnestness in every thought, then with every stroke of the blade, blood will be seen. If not...
If one were to emerge from birth and death [without upholding the precepts],
then all Buddhas would fall into falsehood. (From the *Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miaoye*,
used as a reference) Once a practitioner has cultivated the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation, if they do not maintain the precepts, then despite having faith, they will be defiled by worldly evils.

Because they are invaded and plundered by various defilements, and because the dust of worldly toil is difficult to dispel, the Dharma-body is ruined and one is led to enter into error, failing to attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
If one observes the śrāmaṇera precepts or the full precepts for even a single day and night, one will immediately attain rebirth; therefore, one must certainly maintain the precepts.
Even if one’s past karma is deep and heavy such that it cannot be severed all at once, one should employ skillful means to restrain it, exhorting oneself.

With a focused mind, examine yourself and minimize transgressions. Cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness and realize that worldly pleasures are few while sufferings are many, and that all things are impermanent and subject to decay.
All phenomena are but the toil of defilement; therefore, employ every means to protect and uphold the jewel of the precepts so that they remain pure.
How could one allow the mind to wander according to its impulses? Furthermore, regarding worldly skills, various arts, and even all manner of good and evil deeds—[one must remain detached].
As for those who can divide their thoughts, even if they do not remove themselves to a secluded place, how can they achieve single-mindedness?
If samādhi is not unified, by what means can one be reborn [in the Pure Land]? The ignorant karmic consciousness of sentient beings pervades the entire Dharma-realm;

if one gives rise to even a single thought of worldly mind, one is immediately dragged away by such defilements and demonic hordes. Though a fish may struggle to escape, it can be bound by a single thread; the harm is indeed not small.

If this is so even regarding mental thoughts, how much more so for physical actions? One who cultivates samādhi as swiftly as an arrow hitting its mark does not wait for the exhaustion of karmic retribution;

such a person desires to leap out of the dense forest of afflictions—how could they possibly lose their precepts? The Brahmajāla Sūtra says: "The precepts are like the sun and moon, and also like a jeweled necklace.

By means of them, the multitude of bodhisattvas, as numerous as motes of dust, attain perfect enlightenment. If one is urgent in their practice but lax in the precepts, they will be reborn in evil states.

Among those heading for the realms of rebirth, those who are urgent in both their practice of the Vehicle and their observance of the Precepts will certainly be born in the Pure Land. Those who cultivate the practices for the Pure Land must skillfully protect and maintain themselves to achieve realization within a fixed period.
As the Sūtra says: "Even if evil karma were to possess a physical form and substance, the entirety of the realm of empty space could not contain it. Though [one may commit] a hundred...
Throughout the years, day and night, recite the name of Amitābha ten thousand times. Each single utterance extinguishes the birth and death of eighty billion kalpas.
Yet, the sins thus extinguished are like soil upon a fingernail, while the sins not yet extinguished are like the soil of the great earth.

Only when mindfulness reaches the state of "one mind undisturbed" is one like a strong man breaking through an encirclement, no longer able to be restrained by the three armies. To attain this one mind, one must necessarily...

One must establish the seven periods of practice. In the present practice of mindfulness of the Buddha during these seven periods, for the most part, one creates the causes and conditions for distracted goodness.

Following the crowd in groups, one merely hopes for a sense of bustling activity; as soon as the sound of the Buddha's name ceases, worldly sentiments immediately return. Thus, one vainly wastes time and energy—when has one ever attained the benefit of skillful means?
If one truly resolves the mind to realize the goal within a fixed period, one should first [distinguish between] self-power and other-power.
There are two dharma-gates. One should discern them, direct the mind toward them, and believe with certainty and without doubt.

One should believe in the principle-holding aspect of self-power and the practice-holding aspect of other-power. The *Lianchi Amituo Shuchao* (Lotus Pond Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra) and the *Lingfeng Amituo Yaoyie* (Essential Explanations of Amitābha by Lingfeng) have analyzed these principle-holding and practice-holding aspects in great detail.
If you investigate them with a profound mind, you will certainly be able to decide which path to follow. Be most careful not to...
If the mind is caught between the two sides, it will cause both gates to lose their efficacy. Now, relying on one’s own power (jiriki) approaches the "separate transmission outside the teachings";

although this dharma-gate is superior, it is not a distinct expedient means, for it necessarily requires the severing of delusions before birth [in the Pure Land] occurs—thus remaining identical to the vertical transcendence of the triple world.
Only the dharma-gate of other-power (tariki) relies entirely upon the great power of Amitābha’s vow; there is no need to sever delusions.
Furthermore, they attain rebirth while still carrying their karmic burdens; it is precisely because of this distinction that it is superior.

This most excellent and uniquely extraordinary Dharma-gate is like a weak man who, traveling through the four continents under the power of a Wheel-Turning King, does so not by his own strength, but by the power of the Wheel-Turning King.
Furthermore, it is like an infant who, by relying on and clinging to a compassionate mother, eventually reaches adulthood; this is not through their own power, but because of the mother's power.
A practitioner who places faith in the Dharma-gate of Other-Power and attains a state of faith beyond doubt may set a period of seven days.
If practicing alone, one must strictly observe silence. If there is a companion, one must carefully select them. Seven days prior, one should... [select]... those who are pure.
Select a pure chamber and perform the mantra-recitation and boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*).

Regarding the honored images used for offerings in the practice site (*maṇḍala*), one must conceive of them as the true King of Vows, the Buddha (and this should likewise be done at all times). If the visualization is not authentic, the mind will not be unified.

Once this visualization is purified, first perform prostrations with utmost sincerity (one thousand prostrations, or at least one hundred). Then, invite the Compassionate Honored One to descend upon the practice site, and thereafter remain diligent and earnest.
He made a vow before the Buddha: "I vow to entrust my entire body, mind, and life to the ocean of Amitābha’s great vows.
For seven days, I vow not to give rise to a single thought of worldly things; this means not giving rise to a single thought of calculating or grasping for body, mind, or life.
Having made this vow, he entreated the Buddha with compassion to emit light and gather him in during these seven days.
Receiving [the precepts], one should dwell thus in reliance upon the Buddha. One should set aside all external conditions right where one is and wait quietly for the "seven-day arousal" (*qīqǐ*).
During the seven days of arousal, there is no need to make further vows; one should simply recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Wǎngshēng Zhòu* (Mantra for Rebirth), and hymns of praise to the Buddha.

(On the first day, it is as described above; on the second day, the sūtra and mantra are not used; one rests until one awakens, at which point one immediately holds the Buddha’s name. From this point forward, one should single-mindedly hold the name. In holding the name, one must be neither too lax nor too hurried.
Urgently, without scattering or becoming drowsy, regulate and balance [the mind] until it reaches the middle way. Strive to ensure that the Buddha’s name within the mind is vivid and distinct.
Whether dressing or eating, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, let this single great name be continuous and dense, like breathing itself;
it must not stop for even a moment. If it is mixed with other thoughts for even an instant, then—desiring a single-minded state free from distraction—it is by no means easy.

Upon waking from sleep, the monk Haeju alerted himself and went to visit Old Man Zibai. The Master asked, "For what purpose have you left the household life? He replied, "I seek [the Way]."
"Leave suffering behind," the Master said. "By what method do you leave suffering behind? He replied, "I am dull-witted; I simply recite the Buddha's name.
The Master asked, "Does your recitation of the Buddha’s name ever cease or become interrupted? He replied, "When I close my eyes and fall asleep, I forget it.

The Master rebuked him with a display of majestic power, saying, "If you forget as soon as you close your eyes, then even if you recite the Buddha’s name for ten thousand years, it will be of no use. From this day forward, you must simply sleep."
If one continues the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name even within dreams, there will be a way to escape from suffering.
If, however, one cannot recite the Buddha’s name during sleep and forgets it, then upon waking, one should weep aloud and go straight before the Buddha to prostrate until the blood flows.

One should then recite the name either a thousand times or ten thousand times, exhausting all of one's own strength, and then cease. If one practices in this manner twenty or thirty times, [the benefit will be realized].

Even amidst natural, profound slumber, the Buddha does not cease his activity. Furthermore, among those in the world who practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), whether for twenty or thirty years, or for as long as their lives last, it becomes useless at the moment of death.
This is because they have never maintained the mindful state even within their dreams. Moreover, there is the "Method of Entering Contemplation Before Sleep" by the Venerable Chan Master Ciyun.

Rebirth through Returning (Excerpt by Layman Er-lin):

Rebirth through returning has the recitation of the Buddha’s name as the primary practice and meritorious conduct as the auxiliary. What is meant by meritorious conduct? First, the reading and recitation of Mahāyāna sūtras;
second, the diligent practice of skillful means. Regarding Mahāyāna sūtras: such as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the *Amitābha Sūtra*, and the *Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Gaṇḍavyūha*, the *Vimalakīrti*, the "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra," and other such sūtras;
as well as treatises such as the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Alternatively, one may focus exclusively on various Pure Land texts (such as the works of Yongming Yanshou, Tiantai Zhiyi, Tianru Weize, Hanshan Deqing, Zibo Zhenke, Ouyi Zhixu, and more recently Xingcan, Jueliu, and Chuewu). By means of these, one increases the faculty of faith and thereby becomes fully endowed with the discernment of dharmas.
Having long practiced with diligent mastery and deeply understood the meaning and intent, this constitutes the provisions for rebirth.

As for the expedient means, they are set forth in the *Fú tú shuō* (Illustrated Exposition on Cultivating Merit) composed by the Great Master Lianchi, arranged as follows. Its fourfold analysis states:

If one performs meritorious deeds but does not recite the Buddha’s name, when merit is exhausted, one will sink back into the cycle of rebirth. If one recites the Buddha’s name but does not perform meritorious deeds, there will be much bitterness and hardship on the path.

If one lacks merit and does not recite the Buddha’s name, one will join the multitudes of hell-beings, ghosts, and animals. If one both recites the Buddha’s name and performs meritorious deeds, one will later realize the state of the Honored One with Two Feet.
The categories for performing meritorious deeds are as follows:

being filial and obedient toward one's parents; being loyal and serving one's sovereign; molding and painting images of the Buddha; printing and producing scriptures and making offerings to the Saṃgha;
respectfully attending to teachers and elders; constructing and repairing monasteries; and circulating the Way through the copying of good books.
Prohibit slaughter; purchase and release living beings; feed the hungry; provide clothing for those suffering from cold;
dig wells for public use; repair bridges; pave the paths and stairways; universally distribute tea and soup; care for and treat the sick;
distribute medicine; exonerate the innocent; and commute sentences for criminals.
Caring for the elderly and infirm; nurturing orphaned children; burying the dead and providing coffins;
remitting debts; righteously yielding one's property; returning lost items; relieving the suffering of the sick and averting calamities through prayers;
offering rites to deliver deceased spirits; mediating disputes; and saving human lives.
Regarding the categories of meritorious deeds described above, if they are dedicated through *pariṇāmanā*, all may assist one’s rebirth in the Pure Land.
Not only virtuous actions, but even the arising of a single wholesome thought may be dedicated. If an unwholesome thought arises, one should immediately repent;
this very wholesome thought of repentance may also be dedicated. When the conditions for dedication ripen, the conditions for rebirth will accordingly ripen. If...
One should generate the great resolve and universally dedicate [the merit] for the sake of all sentient beings toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The resulting merit is vast and inconceivable.
This is the great matter at the time of death.

For all practitioners, if you do not steady your conduct during ordinary times, you will most easily find yourself flustered and confused when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives. Not only must your own faith, vows, and practice possess genuine power;

There is the power of the Buddha. At what time, in what place, or with what illness one shall pass away cannot be foreseen by oneself.

If one is sustained by the Buddha’s power, everything encountered will be in accord with the Buddha's capacity, ensuring that one does not fall into the den of worldly toil. Second, there must be the power of merit;

When the patient does not recover, one should recite the Buddha’s name to escort them [to rebirth]. With earnest and sincere devotion, it will indeed be as if one were looking upon one's own illness;

Furthermore, the Patriarch Cizhao established the "Three Doubts and Four Gates" discourse as a diligent admonition for those facing death. What are the Three Doubts?
First, one may doubt that because the karma one has accumulated since birth is extremely heavy and one's practice has been shallow for so many days, one fears not being able to attain rebirth.

Second, one may doubt that one owes debts to others, or have unfulfilled aspirations, or that greed, anger, and ignorance have not yet ceased, fearing thus that one will not attain birth [in the Pure Land].
Third, one may doubt that although one has practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, he will not come to welcome one at the time of death.

Of these two doubts, the former is the greatest obstacle for beginners. If one can have deep faith in the ocean of Amitābha’s vows and receive the encouragement of others, this doubt [will be resolved].
It can be eliminated immediately. Therefore, at the time of death, it is essential to encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This final doubt is an extremely heavy obstacle for a practitioner; if it is not first resolved during one's ordinary life, it will instead increase delusive thoughts at the end.

When one's views are extremely heavy and a grave illness besets the body, one often craves medicine; or, because of taking such medicine, one may recklessly kill living beings, thereby losing one's roots of goodness and finding it difficult to escape karmic retribution.

Naturally, in an instant, one will find lightness and ease, and mindfulness of the Buddha will not be obstructed. Fourth, mindfulness of the Buddha is frequent.

Throughout one's life, it is unavoidable that one will harbor thoughts of family affairs and feel attachment to kin; at the moment of death, because of this, one may mistakenly lose right mindfulness.
If you know that impermanence has arrived, such attachment is of no benefit. Instead, suddenly take up the mindfulness of the Buddha, raising it in every thought-moment.
By raising the mindfulness of the Buddha, you will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land. These three doubts and four barriers are of such vital importance. Therefore, Master Shandao...
Shang said: "When an ordinary person approaches the end of life and wishes to be reborn in the Pure Land, they must not fear death.

Relax the body and mind, and silently recite the Buddha’s name within yourself. As soon as you encounter illness, contemplate impermanence and wait for death with a single-minded focus.
You must instruct your family members and visitors who come before you to recite the Buddha’s name for you;

they must not engage in idle chatter or discuss the affairs of the household, such as its strengths and weaknesses. Furthermore, they need not offer gentle words of consolation or prayers for your well-being. If...

Those who rely on this method will certainly attain rebirth; of this there is no doubt.

By virtue of the Buddha’s compassionate power, their heavy karmic offenses are extinguished and the causes for purity increase. When they approach the end of life, they know for themselves that the time has come;

their bodies are free from the suffering of illness, their minds harbor no attachments, and their thoughts are not inverted. As if entering meditative absorption, the Buddhas and the assembly of sages [appear before them].

(Recite in a low voice: The sixth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the divine eye, such that they cannot see as few as hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The sixth great vow: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha. (Prostrate, while visualizing the sixth vow.

(Recite in a low voice: The seventh vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not possess the divine ear such that they can hear and uphold the teachings spoken by hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Awakened!
With single-minded devotion, prostrate in homage. The Seventh Great Vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads. (Prostrate while visualizing the Seventh Vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The Eighth Vow. If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not possess the knowledge of others' minds, down to the level of knowing the mental thoughts of sentient beings in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. The Eighth Great Vow: The Guide and Teacher, Amitābha Buddha. (Prostrate, while contemplating the Eighth Vow.

(Recite in a low voice: The Ninth Vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not possess the power of spiritual travel (*ṛddhi-pāda*), such that in a single thought-moment they cannot, at the very least, traverse hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands—may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Attaining Perfect Enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate in homage. The Ninth Great Vow: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha. (Prostrate while contemplating the Ninth Vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The Tenth Vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should give rise to thoughts of conceiving an attachment to a self, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
With single-minded devotion, prostrate in homage. The Tenth Great Vow: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha. (Prostrate while visualizing the tenth vow.

(Recite in a low voice: The Eleventh Vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not abide in the stage of certainty (*niyāma*) and necessarily reach extinction (*nirvāṇa*), may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
With single-minded devotion, pay homage. The eleventh great vow: the Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha. (Bowing down, contemplate the eleventh vow.)

(Recite softly: The twelfth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, my radiance should have any limit, such that it does not extend downward to illuminate hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. The twelfth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads. (Bowing down, contemplate the twelfth vow.)
(Recite in a low voice: The thirteenth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, my lifespan should be limited, even down to a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate in homage. The thirteenth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads. (Prostrate, while contemplating the thirteenth vow.)

(Recite softly: The fourteenth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any among the śrāvakas in my land who are able to calculate—even if all the sentient beings in the three-thousandfold world-system were to become pratyekabuddhas and together for hundreds of thousands of kalpas were to reckon and know their number—I would not take supreme enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The fourteenth of the great vows: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha. (Perform prostrations while contemplating the fourteenth vow.)

(Recite softly: Fifteenth Vow. If, when I attain Buddhahood, the lifespan of the devas and humans in my land should be limited, except for those who by their own original vows have mastery over the length of their lives, then may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate in homage. The fifteenth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Leads the Way. (Prostrate, while visualizing the fifteenth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The sixteenth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be even the name of anything unwholesome heard among the devas and humans in my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate yourself. The sixteenth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads. (Prostrate, while visualizing the sixteenth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The seventeenth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the immeasurable Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions were not all to praise and extol my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
With single-minded devotion, pay homage. The seventeenth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads. (Prostrate, while visualizing the seventeenth vow.)

(Recite softly: The Eighteenth Vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be sentient beings of the ten directions who, with a sincere heart, believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land, and even if they recite my name but ten times, yet should not be born there—I shall not attain perfect enlightenment, except for those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the True Dharma."
With single-minded devotion, prostrate in worship. The eighteenth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads. (Prostrate; contemplate the eighteenth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The nineteenth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be sentient beings of the ten directions who have resolved their minds on Bodhi, cultivated various merits, and made a sincere vow desiring to be born in my land, yet at the time of their death I should not appear before them surrounded by a great assembly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. The nineteenth great vow: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha. (Prostrate while visualizing the nineteenth vow.)

(Recite softly: The twentieth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be sentient beings in the ten directions who, upon hearing my name, fix their thoughts upon my land, plant the roots of various virtues, and with a sincere heart dedicate their merits toward rebirth in my land, yet fail to achieve their goal."
I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The twentieth of the twenty great vows: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha. (Prostrate while visualizing the twentieth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The twenty-first vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land do not all fully possess the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The twenty-first great vow: the Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha.
(Prostrate while visualizing the twenty-first vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The twenty-second vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas from other Buddha-lands who come to be born in my land do not ultimately reach the stage of being "one birth away from Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), except for those who, by their own original vows, exercise mastery over their transformations, and for those who, for the sake of sentient beings, have donned the lamp of great vows, accumulated the roots of virtue, and are delivering all beings while roaming through various [realms].

In the Buddha-lands, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices, making offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, and transforming countless sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
establishing them in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, so that they transcend ordinary ranks and attain the practices of the various stages.
I shall practice the virtues of Samantabhadra before me. Should I not do so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The twenty-second great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who leads us across. (Prostrate, while visualizing the twenty-second vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The twenty-third vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, should be unable to travel to countless, immeasurable billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands in the time it takes to eat a single meal while making offerings to all Buddhas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The twenty-third great vow: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha.
(Prostrate while visualizing the twenty-third vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The twenty-fourth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, before the presence of all Buddhas, manifest their roots of virtue, yet the various requisites they seek for making offerings do not appear as they intend, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The twenty-fourth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads.
(Prostrate, while visualizing the twenty-fourth vow.)
(Recite in a low voice: The twenty-fifth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not be able to expound all-knowledge, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The twenty-fifth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads.
(Prostrate, while visualizing the twenty-fifth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The twenty-sixth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not obtain bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The twenty-sixth great vow: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha.
(Prostrate while visualizing the twenty-sixth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The twenty-seventh vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land, as well as all things therein, were not adorned with pure radiance and possessed of exquisite forms and colors so uniquely sublime that they could not be measured—even if sentient beings were to attain the divine eye and yet be unable to clearly discern their names and numbers—I would not take supreme enlightenment.
Awakened!
With single-minded devotion, prostrate yourself. The twenty-seventh of the great vows: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Leads Others Across.
(Prostrate, while visualizing the twenty-seventh vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The twenty-eighth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land—even those of the least merit—should be unable to know or see the tree of the site of enlightenment, with its immeasurable radiance and colors, rising four million *li* high, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The twenty-eighth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads.
(Prostrate while visualizing the twenty-eighth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The twenty-ninth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who receive, read, recite, uphold, and explain the Dharma should not obtain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The nineteenth great vow: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha.
(Prostrate while visualizing the twenty-ninth vow.)
(Recite in a low voice: The thirtieth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land were limited, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The thirtieth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads. (Prostrate, while visualizing the thirtieth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The thirty-first vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, my land is not pure such that it illuminates and reflects all the infinite, countless, and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as clearly as one sees one's own face in a bright mirror—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The thirty-first great vow: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha.
(Prostrate while visualizing the thirty-first vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The thirty-second vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, everything from the ground upward to the palaces and towers in the void—including the ponds, streams, flowering trees, and all the myriad things within my land—were not composed of immeasurable varieties of miscellaneous jewels and hundreds of thousands of kinds of incense, so that they were exquisitely adorned and wondrously beautiful, surpassing those of all devas and humans, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Its fragrance universally perfumes the worlds of the ten directions. Any Bodhisattvas who smell it shall all cultivate the practices of a Buddha.
If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate myself. This is the thirty-second great vow: that Amitābha Buddha, the Guide and Teacher, [shall appear]. (Perform prostrations while visualizing the thirty-two marks.)
(Whispering: The thirty-third vow:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any among the classes of sentient beings in the infinite and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions whose bodies are touched by my light, such that their bodies and minds are not rendered supple..."
Gentle and surpassing those of heaven and humanity—if this were not so, I would not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate in homage. This is the thirty-third great vow: that Amitābha Buddha shall act as the guide who leads others to his land.
(Prostrate, while visualizing the thirty-third vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The thirty-fourth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any among the classes of sentient beings in the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who, upon hearing my name, do not attain the profound *dhāraṇīs* and the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The thirty-fourth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads.
(Prostrate, while visualizing the thirty-fourth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The thirty-fifth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be women in any of the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who, upon hearing my name, rejoice with faith and delight, resolve their minds on Bodhi, and loathe their female form, yet after the end of their lives should they again take on a female appearance, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The thirty-fifth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads.
(Prostrate while visualizing the thirty-fifth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The thirty-sixth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitudes of Bodhisattvas in the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should not always practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) from the end of their lives until they reach the path of Buddhahood—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The thirty-sixth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads. (Prostrate, while visualizing the thirty-sixth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The thirty-seventh vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and people of the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, bowing their heads in worship, and with joy, faith, and delight, practice the bodhisattva path, such that all gods and worldlings do not pay them respect—if this were not so..."
If that be so, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Great Vow, the thirty-seventh, the Guide who leads us across: Amitābha Buddha. (Perform prostrations while visualizing the thirty-seventh vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The thirty-eighth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land who desire clothing should have it appear before them by mere thought—such wondrous robes, as praised by the Buddhas, which accord with the Dharma, appearing spontaneously upon their bodies—if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If there should be anyone who seeks to cut, sew, beat, dye, or wash [the garments], may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The thirty-eighth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads.
(Prostrate while visualizing the thirty-eighth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The thirty-ninth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bliss experienced by the devas and humans in my land should not surpass that of bhikṣus who have exhausted their outflows, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The thirty-ninth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Leads the Way.
(Prostrate while visualizing the thirty-ninth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The fortieth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should wish to see the immeasurable, adorned, and pure buddha-lands of the ten directions, they shall, at that very moment and according to their wishes, behold them all clearly reflected within the precious trees.
Just as a clear mirror reflects the image of one's face, if it were not so, I would not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Forty-First Great Vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Leads and Welcomes. (Prostrate while recollecting the Forty-First Vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The forty-first vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any among the assembly of Bodhisattvas in other lands who, upon hearing my name, do not possess complete and flawless faculties until they attain Buddhahood, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The forty-first great vow: the Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha.
(Prostrate while visualizing the forty-first vow.)

(Recite softly: The forty-second vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitudes of bodhisattvas in other lands who hear my name should not all attain the samādhi of pure liberation and, while abiding in this samādhi, be able to make offerings to immeasurable and inconceivable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in the space of a single thought-moment without losing their concentration.
I vow that if it is not so, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Forty-second Great Vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guiding Teacher. (While bowing, contemplate the Forty-second Vow.)

(Recite softly: The forty-third vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in other lands who hear my name should not, at the end of their lives, be born into noble families—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate. The forty-third great vow: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha. (Perform prostrations while contemplating the forty-third vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The forty-fourth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitude of Bodhisattvas in other lands should hear my name and not leap for joy, cultivating the practices of a Bodhisattva and perfecting the roots of virtue—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. The forty-fourth great vow: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha.
(Prostrate while visualizing the forty-fourth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The forty-fifth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of other lands who hear my name do not all attain the Samādhi of Universal Equality and, while abiding in this samādhi until they reach Buddhahood, constantly see all the infinite and inconceivable Buddhas—if this were not so, I would not take hold of the Buddha-way.
Perfectly Awakened One, I prostrate with single-minded devotion. The forty-fifth great vow: the Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha.
(Prostrate while visualizing the forty-fifth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The forty-sixth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not spontaneously hear whatever Dharma they wish to hear according to their own aspirations, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate in homage. The forty-sixth great vow: The Guiding Teacher, Amitābha Buddha.
(Prostrate while visualizing the forty-sixth vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The forty-seventh vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitudes of bodhisattvas in lands of other directions who hear my name should not immediately attain the stage of non-retrogression, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. The forty-seventh of the great vows: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who leads us forth.
(Prostrate, while visualizing the forty-seventh vow.)

(Recite in a low voice: The forty-eighth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitude of Bodhisattvas in other lands who hear my name should not immediately attain the first, second, or third stage of dharma-patience, and should not immediately attain non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. At that time, the Dharma-treasury...
After Kṣema had spoken these vows, at that very moment the entire earth shook in six ways, and the heavens rained down exquisite flowers which fell upon him.
From the sky, voices praised him, saying: "You shall certainly and surely attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. The forty-eighth great vow: Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who Welcomes and Leads.
(Bowing down, contemplate the forty-eighth vow.)
The Essentials for Cultivating Rebirth in the West (Concluded).

This was carved into woodblocks by Xiuzixi to accumulate merit, universally wishing that all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm— the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence— may together cultivate the pure karma,
maintain clear and correct mindfulness, ensure their certain rebirth there, and dwell eternally in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
Recorded by the Jiangbei Institute for Carving Scriptures during the second month of winter in the tenth year of the Guangxu era.
